objectives: Trace a DMA transfer's data path.
Recognize when each I/O model wins.

slides.title: Interrupts, the asynchronous mechanism
slides.body:
When hardware needs the CPU's attention (network packet arrived, disk read completed, key pressed), it raises an **interrupt** — a hardware signal that suspends the current task + jumps to a kernel handler.

Process (simplified x86):
1. Device asserts IRQ line.
2. CPU completes current instruction.
3. CPU saves RIP + RFLAGS, looks up IDT (Interrupt Descriptor Table) for IRQ handler.
4. Jumps to handler (kernel code).
5. Handler does minimum (acknowledge device, queue work for a 'softirq' or kernel thread), returns.
6. CPU restores state, resumes interrupted task.

Cost: ~1µs per interrupt on modern CPUs. Not free — but vastly better than polling at the kernel's rate.

**Top-half / bottom-half split**: the top half runs in interrupt context (preempts everything; must be fast). It schedules a bottom half (softirq, tasklet, work queue) to run with normal priority, doing the actual work. Network packet handling is the canonical example: top half ACKs the device + pulls the packet to RAM; bottom half does TCP processing.

slides.title: DMA: hardware-direct data movement
slides.body:
Without DMA: every byte moved between disk + RAM goes through the CPU (`mov` instructions). On a 5GB/s NVMe, this would saturate the CPU just on copying.

**DMA (Direct Memory Access)**: dedicated controller moves data between device + RAM without CPU involvement. CPU sets up the transfer (source addr, dest addr, length); DMA controller runs autonomously; CPU is free to do other work; interrupt fires when transfer completes.

Modern NVMe SSDs: PCIe transactions handle the data path; the CPU just submits commands + handles completion interrupts. 5GB/s read throughput costs the CPU ~1% utilization (mostly interrupt handling, not data movement).

This is the substrate of modern I/O performance: the CPU never sees the bytes. The same pattern applies to GPUs (cuMemcpyAsync is DMA), network cards (NIC DMA descriptors), USB controllers.

slides.title: Polled vs interrupt-driven I/O — when each wins
slides.body:
**Polled** (busy-wait): CPU repeatedly checks if device is ready. Low latency (no interrupt overhead). High CPU cost (CPU is busy doing nothing useful while polling).

**Interrupt-driven**: CPU does other work; interrupt fires when ready. Latency: ~1µs handler overhead. Throughput: limited by interrupt rate the CPU can handle.

The crossover:
- **Very high IOPS** (>1M/sec on NVMe, 10M+ packets/sec on network): interrupt overhead becomes the bottleneck. DPDK/SPDK switch to polling for the data plane.
- **Low-rate I/O** (typical disk, network): interrupts are cheaper than polling.
- **Mixed**: NIC interrupt coalescing — accumulate packets, fire one interrupt for many. Throws away some latency for lower CPU.

Production: typical app uses interrupt-driven (the OS default). High-frequency-trading + AAA gaming + custom networking move to polling. The whole 'kernel bypass' ecosystem (DPDK, XDP, SPDK) is about replacing interrupts with polling for the data plane.

question.question: Derive when polling beats interrupts
question.goal: Interrupt cost $C_i$ (1µs). Poll cost $C_p$ per check (50ns). Device rate $R$ ops/sec.

steps.prompt: Interrupt mode total CPU per second: $R \cdot C_i$. Polling mode (poll once per check): assume 1 poll per op = $R \cdot C_p$. Crossover when $R \cdot C_p \geq R \cdot C_i$ — never with these parameters. Why might polling still win?

options: Polling burns CPU even when no work is available — the comparison isn't symmetric.

hints: Interrupt cost is per-event; polling cost is per-poll (more polls than events).
steps.reveal: Polling polls many times to catch each event; total polling cost is much higher than $R \cdot C_p$. Crossover depends on poll frequency vs event rate.

steps.prompt: At very high $R$ (~1M/sec), interrupt cost approaches 100% CPU. Why does polling win?

options: $R \cdot C_i = 10^6 \cdot 10^{-6}$ s = 1 second of CPU per second of wallclock — fully saturated by interrupts. Polling, even busy-polling, can be cheaper per op once you're below the 'one poll per arrival' density.

hints: At 1M/sec interrupt rate, all CPU goes to handling them.
steps.reveal: Interrupt saturation at $R \geq 1/C_i$. For $C_i = 1$µs, that's $10^6$/sec. Above this, polling wins because per-poll cost is lower than per-interrupt cost AND you can amortize across many ops.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Polling wins when interrupt rate would saturate the CPU}}$$ DPDK + SPDK exist for exactly this regime. Below: interrupts win because they don't burn CPU when idle. The crossover is around 100K-1M events/sec depending on hardware.

question.question: A 10Gbps network card receives 1.5M packets/sec at small-packet workload. Default mode: one interrupt per packet. CPU is overwhelmed. Best mitigation:
options: Enable interrupt coalescing — accumulate N packets per interrupt.
question.explanation: Interrupt coalescing accumulates multiple packet arrivals into a single interrupt. The NIC waits ~50-100µs to batch arrivals; CPU handles N packets per interrupt instead of 1. Trade-off: small latency increase (~50µs) for dramatically reduced interrupt overhead. Production network cards all support this; many auto-tune it.

hints: What's the cost trade in batching interrupts?
slides.workedSolution: Coalescing reduces interrupts/sec at the cost of small added latency. At 1.5M pps with no coalescing, that's 1.5M interrupts/sec — saturating the CPU. With 10:1 coalescing, 150K interrupts/sec — manageable. Adds ~50µs latency. For non-latency-critical workloads (web serving), big win.

question.prompt: Your team is building a software load balancer that needs to handle 10M packets/sec. The kernel TCP stack can sustain ~1M pps per core. Walk through whether to use DPDK (kernel bypass) vs scaling kernel-based + the trade-offs.
Explain in two or three sentences why DMA + interrupts together enable modern I/O.
question.rubric: Mentions that DMA moves data without CPU; interrupts notify the CPU when transfers complete; together the CPU only does setup + completion, never the bulk data movement; this is what makes 5GB/s NVMe + 100Gbps NICs feasible on a single CPU core.
